record_identity.title: Hanover Institute influence campaign targeting chatbot retrieval

incident_identity.date_basis: Earliest preserved registry publication date; campaign start and duration remain unresolved.

summary: AI Incident Database incident 1659 and contemporaneous reporting describe an Israeli government-backed communications campaign that created the Hanover Institute for Public Policy, published large volumes of policy-style material designed for chatbot retrieval, and obtained citations from ChatGPT and Perplexity in some neutral-query tests. The evidence establishes deliberate optimisation of a synthetic institutional source for AI retrieval and observed citation in some tests. It does not establish model-weight manipulation, universal retrieval, control of the cited platforms, or a settled VIGIL failure classification.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: AI Incident Database incident 1659 and contemporaneous reporting describe an Israeli government-backed communications campaign that created the Hanover Institute for Public Policy, published large volumes of policy-style material designed for chatbot retrieval, and obtained citations from ChatGPT and Perplexity in some neutral-query tests. The evidence establishes deliberate optimisation of a synthetic institutional source for AI retrieval and observed citation in some tests. It does not establish model-weight manipulation, universal retrieval, control of the cited platforms, or a settled VIGIL failure classification.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: AI systems increasingly mediate evidence discovery and public knowledge. A source can be publicly accessible, machine-readable and citation-rich while its apparent institutional identity, independence or epistemic authority is deliberately manufactured. VIGIL should preserve this as an unresolved provenance-and-authority observation until the current failure taxonomy is reconciled against the mechanism. The governance question is whether source availability, presentation and retrieval optimisation can be mistaken for independently established source authority or provenance.
